title: Writing Your Own Materials

pts: Original materials become worthwhile when existing coursebooks or resources genuinely don't fit a specific learner group's needs closely enough.
This connects to Unit 13's coursebook-adaptation and Unit 65's ESP-materials principles, taken to their natural conclusion.
Writing materials well is a genuinely distinct craft skill, worth developing deliberately rather than assuming it follows automatically from good teaching.

v: The current coursebook unit; a profile of the class

items: Choose a coursebook unit you will teach soon.
List what fits your learners and what does not (topic, level, genre, context, task type).
Decide for each gap: omit, adapt (Unit 13), find an existing resource, or write something new.
Estimate the time each option would take.
Write new material only where adaptation or finding would not meet the need.
In a subject team, share the decisions so that one teacher writes and others pilot.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: A decision table (written for this book):

lines: Reading text about a ski holiday → learners have no experience of snow → adapt: replace with a text about a hill-station trip written for the class.
Grammar exercise on ‘used to’ → fits well → keep.
Speaking task: ‘discuss your favourite restaurant’ → many learners rarely eat out → write a new task about the school canteen menu.

blocks.x: Writing is expensive in time. It is worth it when the gap is real and the material will be reused.

body: Purpose: to show the options before writing. Content: four doors labelled ‘omit’, ‘adapt’, ‘find’ and ‘write’, with a teacher holding a coursebook deciding which to open; the ‘write’ door is last in the row. Style: simple, clear. Board version: four rectangles with labels.

items: DIKSHA (free, Government of India) and StoryWeaver (free, Pratham Books) for existing materials to check before writing.

blocks.x: A decision table in the planning notebook.

points.sub: Materials serve a purpose, not vice versa
pts: Design materials backward from a specific learning aim, echoing Unit 9's lesson-planning principle at the materials-design level.
Materials created without a clear aim in mind tend toward generic, unfocused content that doesn't efficiently serve any particular goal.
This is the same discipline Unit 28's task design demands, applied to the concrete artefacts a lesson will actually use.

v: A lesson aim; a blank design sheet

items: Write the lesson aim as a can-do statement.
Describe what learners will produce or do by the end of the material.
Work backwards: what language, input and support do they need to get there?
Only now decide on the text type, task and layout.
Check every section of the draft against the aim and cut anything that does not serve it.
Swap design sheets with a colleague and ask them to guess the aim from the draft material alone.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: A design sheet (written for this book):

lines: Aim: learners can write a short notice announcing a school event, including date, time, place and a call to action.
End product: a notice for the school board.
Needed: a model notice; key phrases (‘All students are invited…’, ‘Please register by…’); a checklist.
Cut: a crossword on sports vocabulary; it was fun but did not serve the aim.

blocks.x: This is the backward design discipline of lesson planning (Unit 9) and task design (Unit 28) applied to the artefacts learners will use.

body: Purpose: to show aim-first design. Content: a road from right to left: a finished notice on the right (‘the aim’), then road signs pointing back to ‘model’, ‘phrases’ and ‘checklist’, and a teacher starting on the left with a clear map. Style: flat illustration. Board version: an arrow from the aim back to three steps.

items: Google Docs (free) for a reusable design-sheet template.

pts: Apply Unit 28's task-design criteria directly — does this material create a genuine gap or purpose for language use, not just practice for its own sake?
Materials that only practise pre-specified language forms, with no communicative outcome, replicate the limitations Unit 28 warns against in exercise design generally.
This is where TBLT theory and concrete materials-writing craft meet directly.

v: 45 minutes to write; 30 minutes to use

items: Take a practice exercise with no communicative outcome, for example ‘Complete the sentences with the correct form’.
Identify the language it practises.
Rewrite it so that learners need that language to find or share information they do not have.
Create two versions (A and B) with different information.
Add an outcome: a decision, a completed chart or a solved problem.
Turn a gap-fill into an opinion-gap task: learners rank options and must agree.
Support: provide question frames on the A and B cards.
Challenge: learners write their own B card for a new partner.

lines: Complete: The bus ___ (leave) at 7.30.
Card A: You have the bus times from Mysuru to Bengaluru. Your partner has the train times. Together, decide the fastest way to arrive before 11.00.
A: What time does the first train leave?
B: At 6.15. It arrives at 9.05. And the bus?

blocks.x: Learners use the present simple for timetables naturally because they need it. This is the step from exercise to task (Ellis 2003).

body: Purpose: to show an information-gap design. Content: two half-cards, A with a bus timetable and B with a train timetable, and a jigsaw piece joining them labelled ‘decision’. Style: clean design. Board version: two boxes with a question mark between them.

items: Canva for Education (free for teachers) for A/B card templates.

blocks.x: Handwritten cards cut from scrap paper.

pts: Apply Unit 28's dual grading levers — language complexity and task complexity — deliberately when writing new materials from scratch.
Piloting materials with a real class before wider use reveals grading misjudgements that pure desk-based design can miss.
This connects to Unit 57's washback-piloting principle, applied to teaching materials rather than formal tests specifically.

v: A new material; a pilot record sheet

items: Before piloting, rate the material on two dials: language difficulty and task difficulty (Unit 28), each from 1 to 5.
Pilot it with one class.
Note where learners stopped, asked for help or finished early.
Decide which dial caused each problem.
Adjust only one dial at a time for the next version.
Pilot with two classes at different levels to find the range the material suits.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: A pilot record (written for this book):

lines: Stage 2: learners stuck on ‘reservation’, ‘departure’ → language dial too high → add a glossary box.
Stage 3: learners understood but could not compare four options at once → task dial too high → reduce to three options.
Stage 4: finished in 8 minutes instead of 15 → fine; add an optional extension.

blocks.x: Desk design rarely predicts every problem. As with test piloting in Unit 57, a short trial shows what the design missed.

body: Purpose: to show separate grading of language and task. Content: two dials on a control panel, ‘language’ and ‘task’, each with a pointer; a teacher adjusts one while the other stays still. Style: clean infographic. Board version: two semicircles with needles.

items: Google Forms (free) for a two-question learner exit slip on difficulty.

blocks.x: Thumbs up, sideways or down from learners at the end of each stage.

pts: Use corpus tools (Unit 58) to verify that invented example sentences and dialogues reflect genuinely natural language use.
Authentic or corpus-informed materials avoid the artificially clean 'textbook English' Unit 13 warned against auditing for.
This is one of the most concrete, high-value applications of this tier's corpus-linguistics work.

v: Draft example sentences or a dialogue; internet access

items: Underline three phrases in your draft that you are unsure about.
Check each one in a corpus tool (Unit 58).
Compare frequency and typical collocations with your version.
Revise any phrase that is rare or unnatural.
Add one frequent, natural chunk you found to the material.
Where corpus tools are not available, compare with two or three authentic texts of the same genre.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: Checking a draft dialogue (written for this book):

lines: Draft: ‘I have a doubt, madam.’
Corpus check: ‘I have a question’ and ‘Can I ask something?’ are far more common in international English; ‘I have a doubt’ is characteristic of Indian English.
Decision: keep ‘I have a doubt’ for an Indian classroom dialogue, but teach ‘I have a question’ as the internationally common form and discuss the difference.

blocks.x: Corpus evidence can inform choices about variety as well as naturalness. Unit 74 discusses World Englishes in depth.

body: Purpose: to show corpus checking in practice. Content: a laptop screen with a simple concordance of ‘have a question’, lines aligned on the key phrase, beside a draft worksheet with one phrase circled. Style: realistic screen. Board version: three aligned sentences with the key phrase underlined.

items: SkELL (Sketch Engine for Language Learning, free) for example sentences and collocations [VERIFY current access].
COCA (Corpus of Contemporary American English; free limited access with registration) for frequency data.

blocks.x: A small collection of authentic texts in the same genre, marked for useful phrases.

body: Corpora of Indian English exist, including the Indian component of the International Corpus of English (ICE-India). Evidence from such corpora can help teachers decide which Indian English features are widely used in educated writing [VERIFY current availability of ICE-India for teachers].

pts: Apply Unit 54's genre-based teaching cycle structure directly when designing materials meant to build toward independent genre production.
Materials should model coherent, cohesive discourse (Unit 52), not just grammatically correct isolated sentences.
This raises the transferability of what learners practise toward genuine, connected real-world language use.

blocks.x: A model text with a teaching purpose

v: The target genre; a checklist of its stages and features

items: Choose the genre learners will produce (Unit 54), for example a formal complaint email.
List its stages and key language features.
Write a model text that shows each stage clearly and uses cohesive devices naturally (Unit 52).
Add margin labels for stages and highlight two or three features.
Create a deconstruction task that asks learners to find stages and features themselves.
Write a weaker second version so learners can compare and improve it.
Support: provide stage labels to match to paragraphs.
Challenge: learners annotate the model without labels.

blocks.x: Part of a model complaint email (written for this book):

lines: [Purpose] I am writing to complain about the delay in delivering my order no. 4452.
[Background] I placed the order on 3 March and was told it would arrive within five days.
[Problem] However, it has now been three weeks, and I have received no update despite two phone calls.
[Request] I would therefore be grateful if you could deliver the item or refund the full amount by 30 March.

blocks.x: Each sentence both carries meaning and teaches a move in the genre. The cohesive words (However, therefore) are placed where they do real work.

body: Purpose: to show a model text with its stages visible. Content: an email on the right with coloured margin brackets on the left labelled Purpose, Background, Problem, Request; two cohesive words circled. Style: clean, textbook. Board version: four bracketed paragraphs with labels.

items: Google Docs (free) with comments for annotation.

blocks.x: A model text written on chart paper with coloured-pen labels.

pts: Clear, uncluttered layout and appropriate visual support materially affect how usable and accessible written materials actually are.
This connects to Unit 23's inclusive-design principles — accessible layout benefits all learners, not only those with specific additional needs.
Good visual design is a genuine, learnable craft skill, worth deliberate attention alongside the linguistic content itself.

v: One of your worksheets; a layout checklist

items: Look at the worksheet from arm’s length. Where does your eye go first?
Check it against a short layout checklist (see model language).
Mark every problem in a different colour.
Redesign it on a fresh sheet.
Ask two learners which version is easier to use, and why.
Audit a worksheet for photocopying: does it still work in black and white on poor paper?
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: A layout checklist (written for this book, drawing on inclusive-design principles from Unit 23):

lines: Clear title and aim at the top.
Instructions short, numbered and in bold, separate from content.
A plain, large font; no text over pictures.
White space between tasks; one task per box.
Pictures that help meaning, not only decoration.
Works when photocopied in black and white.

blocks.x: Clear layout helps every learner, including those with visual, reading or attention difficulties. Research on multimedia learning suggests that removing extraneous material can support understanding (Mayer 2009).

body: Purpose: to contrast cluttered and clear layout. Content: two worksheet thumbnails; the left crowded with clip art, mixed fonts and dense text; the right with a clear title, numbered boxes and white space. Style: side-by-side comparison. Board version: two rectangles, one filled with scribbles, one with neat boxes.

items: Canva for Education (free for teachers) or Google Docs (free) for clean templates.

blocks.x: A ruler, a pencil and a handwritten worksheet with clear boxes.

body: Before photocopying fifty sheets, photocopy one. Many worksheets that look clear on screen become unreadable after a school photocopier, especially if they use pale colours or photographs.

points.sub: Treat them as a living resource
pts: Pilot new materials with a real class and revise based on what actually happens, echoing Unit 9's reflective-practice cycle directly.
Keep a simple record of what worked and what needed adjustment, building an increasingly refined resource over successive uses.
This closes the loop: materials-writing, like teaching itself, improves through the same disciplined, iterative reflection this series has built throughout.

v: A folder or digital drive; a revision log

items: Store every piece of original material in one folder with a version number.
After each use, add three lines to the revision log: what worked, what did not, what to change.
Make the change before filing it for next time.
Once a term, review the file with a colleague and share the best materials.
Where possible, share final versions under an open licence.
A school or DIET materials bank where teachers contribute and rate materials.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: A revision log entry (written for this book):

lines: Bus and train gap task, v2, Class 8C, 14 July. Worked: all pairs reached a decision. Did not work: B cards too dense. Change: move train times into a table. Filed as v3.

blocks.x: Materials, like lessons, improve through the reflective cycle introduced in Unit 9 and formalized as action research in Unit 67.

body: Purpose: to show iterative improvement. Content: three worksheets fanned out labelled v1, v2 and v3, each slightly clearer, with sticky notes of feedback between them. Style: warm, realistic. Board version: three rectangles with arrows.

items: Google Drive (free) with version history for shared materials files.

blocks.x: A box file with plastic sleeves, one per material, and a revision log sheet on the front.

body: Choose one exercise you use often that has no communicative outcome. Rewrite it with an information or opinion gap, pilot it with one class, record what happens, and produce a second version within a week.

dek: Unit 69 of 100: closing this stretch of Tier III with the natural culmination of accumulated expertise — designing original teaching materials with genuine craft.

aims.x: Teachers write materials all the time: a worksheet for tomorrow, a role-card set, a reading text about the local market. This unit treats that everyday activity as a craft. It shows how to decide when original materials are worth writing, how to design them from an aim, how to build in communicative purpose, genre and natural language, how to lay them out clearly, and how to improve them through piloting.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: decide when writing new materials is justified rather than adapting existing ones;
design materials backwards from a specific learning aim;
build a genuine communicative purpose or gap into a worksheet or task;
grade the language and the task separately and check both through piloting;
use corpus tools to check that invented examples sound natural;
write materials that model connected discourse and support genre-based work;
apply principles of clear, accessible layout;
keep a simple revision record so that materials improve with each use.

why: Why this matters. Every principle in this series — genre, task design, assessment, discourse — converges in the concrete, practical craft of writing a lesson's actual materials.

background.x: Materials development became a recognized field of study in ELT from the 1990s, led in particular by Brian Tomlinson, whose edited volumes brought together principles and research on how materials can support acquisition (Tomlinson 2011). Tomlinson argues that materials should achieve impact, help learners feel at ease, expose them to language in authentic use, and give them opportunities to use the language for communication. David Jolly and Rod Bolitho (1998) described materials writing as a sequence of steps, from identifying a need through exploring the language, finding a context, designing activities and producing the physical material, to use in class and evaluation.

Teachers’ own materials are rarely published, but they are often the most closely fitted to learners. Ian McGrath (2016) discusses how teachers evaluate, adapt and create materials, and how the choice depends on time, resources and learners’ needs. Freda Mishan and Ivor Timmis (2015) show how principles from second language acquisition, genre and corpus research can inform everyday materials design. Nigel Harwood (2010) brings together research on how materials are designed and used.

In India, teachers work with state textbooks and, increasingly, with national digital resources such as DIKSHA. NCF 2023 encourages teachers to use and create local, contextually relevant materials, and NEP 2020 emphasizes learning in and through local contexts and languages (NCERT 2023; Ministry of Human Resource Development 2020). A worksheet about the weekly santhe (market) in a Karnataka village, or a bilingual glossary for a science reading, can connect English to learners’ lives in a way no global coursebook can. Openly licensed materials, for example those published under Creative Commons licences, also allow teachers to adapt and share legally.

This unit draws together principles from across the book: coursebook adaptation (Unit 13), task design (Unit 28), genre (Unit 54), cohesion (Unit 52), corpus tools (Unit 58), inclusive design (Unit 23) and ESP materials (Unit 65). Unit 80 later examines materials design principles from a theoretical and research perspective.

items: Design sheet. An aim-first design with a clear end product and evidence of cutting material that does not serve the aim.
Task redesign. An exercise rewritten as a task with a gap and an outcome, with A/B versions.
Pilot record. Notes from one pilot showing which grading dial caused each difficulty and how it was adjusted.
Revision log. At least two versions of one material with reasons for each change.
Which of your own materials do you reuse most? Why do they work?
When have you written something new when adapting would have been enough?
How do you check that invented example language sounds natural?
Which of your worksheets would you redesign after the layout audit?
How could your learners’ home languages appear usefully in your materials?
How could your school share good materials across teachers and years?

perm: All decision tables, design sheets, tasks, model texts, checklists and revision logs are written for this book. When adapting published or online materials, check copyright; openly licensed resources (for example under Creative Commons) may be adapted within their licence terms and must be attributed. Screenshots of DIKSHA, StoryWeaver, SkELL, COCA, Canva or Google tools require permission or replacement with original illustrations.

terms.def: Planning that begins with the intended outcomes, then decides how they will be assessed, and only then chooses activities (Wiggins and McTighe 2005); also called backward planning.
A quick check of a word or phrase in a corpus before teaching it, to confirm how common and natural it is; for example, comparing I have a doubt with I have a question.
Adjusting the difficulty of materials or tasks for a group of learners, by changing the language demand, the task demand, or both, often one at a time so the cause of difficulty is clear.
An activity in which learners hold different information and must communicate to complete a task, such as finding differences between two pictures or completing a timetable.

The visual arrangement of text, headings, images, white space and instructions on a page or screen; clear, consistent layout makes materials easier to follow, especially when worksheets are photocopied in black and white.

The field and practice of producing, evaluating and adapting materials for language learning, informed by research on second language acquisition; it became a recognized area of ELT in the 1990s, led by Brian Tomlinson.
An example text written or chosen to show the stages and language features of a target genre, which learners analyse before writing their own, for example a model formal complaint letter.
Trying out new materials or a test with a small group before full use, in order to identify problems and revise them.

A short record kept with teaching materials in which teachers note, after each use, what worked, what did not and what to change. It turns materials development into a continuous, shared improvement process.

The concrete result that a task produces, such as a completed map, a decision, a list or a poster. A clear outcome gives the task a purpose and allows teacher and learners to judge whether it was achieved.
